author: Platform Documentation
deck: Most objects in this CMS can be created and published by an agent alone. A few can't — and the difference is deliberate, not accidental.
description: How the platform decides which objects an agent can publish unassisted and which ones require a human decision first.

public.body: An agent can create a page, adjust a navigation menu, or publish an article without asking anyone first. Try the same thing on a handful of other object types, and the system will refuse — not because something broke, but because that type is built to wait for a person. Knowing which is which, and why, saves a lot of confused troubleshooting.
public.title: Two agents, two very different outcomes

public.body: Every object type in the CMS carries its own publish policy, decided in advance, not guessed at run time. Most types — the structural, low-risk ones — are autonomous: an agent that creates a valid, checked object can publish it directly, the same way a person with the right role could. A smaller set of higher-stakes types requires a human's explicit approval before anything ships, regardless of who wrote the content.
public.title: Most types are autonomous; a few aren't

public.body: An approval isn't a blanket "yes" that covers whatever comes next. It's tied to the exact thing being approved: the specific object, at a specific version of its content, doing a specific action — publishing it now, scheduling it, or taking it down. If the content changes after approval, or someone tries a different action than the one that was approved, the approval no longer applies. It has to be given again, against the new reality.
public.title: An approval is pinned to one exact action

public.body: Practically, this means an agent working on an approval-gated object can still do almost everything up to the final step: draft it, validate it, check it against the site's own rules, get it into a reviewable state. What it can't do is make that last move alone. And even when a human executes that final publish, the platform still checks they're carrying the right role for it — authorship and authorization are checked separately.
public.title: What an agent can and can't do alone

public.body: The point isn't to slow an agent down for its own sake. It's to make sure the handful of changes that matter most — the ones a reader or a business decision actually depends on — always have a person's deliberate decision behind them, while everything else keeps moving at agent speed.
public.title: Why the friction is there on purpose
